title: Collapse of rational recurrence systems to single recurrences
formal: Does every rationally recursive sequence \(u:\mathbb N\to\mathbb Q\) admit a single finite-depth rational recurrence? Explicitly, for every such \(u\), must there exist an integer \(d\geq1\) and polynomials \(A,B\in\mathbb Q[y_{0},\ldots,y_{d-1}]\) such that, for all \(n\geq0\), \[B(u_{n},\ldots,u_{n+d-1})\ne0,\qquad u_{n+d}=\frac{A(u_{n},\ldots,u_{n+d-1})}{B(u_{n},\ldots,u_{n+d-1})}?\]

source_formulation.text: Unlike in the case of polynomial updates, we conjecture that for rational updates we do have such a collapse.
source_formulation.caption: Complete selected source sentence; PDF p. 3

context:
For linear updates, finite mutual systems can be represented by single finite-depth linear recurrences. For polynomial updates the corresponding statement fails: the source recalls polynomially recursive sequences that have no single polynomial recurrence. Allowing division gives a distinct conjecture about expressive power.

Theorem 6 establishes a scalar rational recurrence when the original initial values are independent formal variables and the evolving values are rational functions of those variables. This is a theorem over a function field. It does not cover every fixed rational specialization of the initial vector.

The source explicitly explains why its symbolic result does not prove Conjecture 1: a denominator in the resulting scalar recurrence may vanish after substituting particular rational initial values, even when the original mutual system remains well-defined. An identity obtained by clearing denominators also need not specify a valid next value at those windows.

The source relates an effective version of the collapse to checking whether polynomially recursive sequences are identically zero and whether two such sequences agree everywhere. Those consequences require a suitable constructive conversion; they should not be built into this purely existential conjecture.
why: Asks whether auxiliary state increases the expressive power of rational recurrences, or whether finite memory of the observed sequence always suffices. It is a basic structural question about discrete algebraic dynamics and the sequence models underlying weighted and polynomial automata.
status_note: Read the full conference Conjecture 1, rational-recursion definitions, Theorem 6 and its specialization discussion, and the corresponding author-version formulation. Checked arXiv revision history and searched through 12 September 2026 for subsequent work; no resolution of the rational-initial-value collapse was found. The symbolic theorem, implicit polynomial identities and efficient conversion are kept distinct from the stated existence claim.

sentences: A rationally recursive sequence is one coordinate of a finite system whose next state is a rational function of its current state.
The conjecture asks whether finitely many past values of that coordinate always suffice to generate its next value.
All coefficients and initial values are rational, and every denominator must remain nonzero along the sequence.
A scalar recurrence may depend on the particular initial vector, but must work at every step.
The known theorem with symbolic initial values does not settle the numerical case because specialization can make its denominators vanish.

definitions:
Here \(\mathbb N=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\). A sequence \(u\) is rationally recursive if there are an integer \(k\geq1\), rational initial values \(a_{1},\ldots,a_{k}\), and rational functions
\[F_{i}=P_{i}/Q_{i}\in\mathbb Q(x_{1},\ldots,x_{k})\qquad(1\leq i\leq k)\]
that generate a state sequence \(\mathbf z_{n}\in\mathbb Q^{k}\) by
\[\mathbf z_{0}=(a_{1},\ldots,a_{k}),\qquad
z_{n+1,i}=F_{i}(\mathbf z_{n}),\qquad u_{n}=z_{n,1}.\]
All components are updated simultaneously from the preceding state. Each \(P_{i},Q_{i}\) is a finite polynomial with rational coefficients, \(Q_{i}\) is not the zero polynomial, and \(Q_{i}(\mathbf z_{n})\ne0\) for every \(i,n\). The other coordinates are auxiliary sequences.

The proposed scalar recurrence uses only the last \(d\) values of \(u\), in their stated order. Its coefficients are rational constants. It has no separate access to the index \(n\), the hidden coordinates, an externally supplied clock, or a rule that changes with \(n\). The first \(d\) actual values of \(u\) are its initial data.

The quantifiers permit \(d,A,B\) to depend on the entire sequence, including the original rational initial values. They must then work at every step. There is no requirement for one scalar recurrence to work uniformly for all initial vectors of a given mutual-update system, and no prescribed bound on \(d\), degree or coefficient size.

Denominators must be nonzero at every state or scalar window where the chosen fraction is evaluated. Algebraic cancellation may be used when choosing a fraction representation, but a recurrence is not allowed to evaluate \(0/0\), assign it an arbitrary value, or switch formulas to handle exceptional windows. The scalar recurrence must hold from \(n=0\), after its initial \(d\) values, rather than only on an unspecified eventual tail.

The claim is semantic existence of a finite recurrence over \(\mathbb Q\). It does not require an algorithm for finding one, a time bound for conversion, or an algorithm that checks whether an arbitrary proposed rational-update system avoids division by zero. The input class already consists of systems whose entire orbit is defined.

A scalar recurrence can always be expressed as a finite mutual system by retaining its finitely many preceding values as state. Thus the displayed direction is precisely the missing direction in the source’s equality of the two sequence classes.
answer_criterion: Prove the displayed recurrence exists for every well-defined rationally recursive sequence over \(\mathbb Q\), or give such a sequence and prove that no finite \(d\) and no rational function with nonvanishing denominators along its windows can generate it in this way. A recurrence only for generic initial conditions, an implicit polynomial relation, or a rule with exceptional undefined evaluations does not settle the conjecture.
